  "text": "## Perceptions of similarity
In the presence of ambiguous similarity information, participants in a positive mood were expected to perceive themselves as more similar to upward comparison targets relative to downward comparison targets. To test these hypotheses, participant responses to the three similarity questions were averaged (alpha = .87) and this similarity index was submitted to a 2(mood: positive vs. neutral) × 2(direction: upward vs. downward) × 2(similarity cue: unambiguous vs. ambiguous sign of distinctive similarity) ANOVA.

As shown in Table 2, the significant main effects of similarity cue, F(1,88) = 55.38, p < .001 and direction, F(1, 88) = 22.80, p < .001, were qualified by the two-way interaction effects of direction and mood, F(1,88) = 18.14, p < .001, and similarity cue and direction, F(1,88) = 26.20, p < .001. These were further qualified by the significant three-way interaction effect, F(1, 88) = 15.32, p < .001.

As shown in Table 2, and as revealed by planned comparisons, in the presence of ambiguous information, participants in a positive mood rated upward comparison targets as more similar to the self than downward comparison targets, F(1, 94) = 53.17, p < .001. However, when similarity information was unambiguous, participants rated the upward and downward comparison targets as equally similar to the self, F(1, 94) = 1.00, p > .05. Therefore, participants in a positive mood did not respond in a biased manner. In contrast, in the neutral mood condition, when information was ambiguous, direction of comparison did not influence ratings of similarity, F(1, 94) = .31, p = .58. Identical effects emerged when the information was unambiguous, F(1, 94) = 1.50, p = .83.

We further analyzed the relations between similarity and self-evaluations in each of the conditions. When information was unambiguous, self and other attractiveness were significantly related in the positive, r(24) = .87, p < .001, and neutral mood, r(24) = .53, p = .008, reflecting assimilation of self. In the ambiguous conditions, self-evaluations were not correlated with ratings of target attractiveness in either the positive or neutral mood, ps > .84. However, in a positive mood, ratings of similarity were correlated with ratings of other attractiveness, r(24) = .70, p < .001. In a neutral mood, this correlation was not significant, p > .9. These results suggest that the presence of ambiguous similarity cues allows those in a positive mood to see others in self-serving ways.4

## Discussion
Supporting our hypothesis, positive mood was associated with biased interpretations of ambiguous information. When comparison targets were superior, sharing an esthetic preference was regarded as reflecting greater similarity, similarity was related to self-evaluations, and participants assimilated their self-evaluations to the targets. When comparison targets were inferior, sharing an esthetic preference was regarded as not reflecting similarity and participants did not respond to the targets. In this way, the resolution of ambiguity in a positive mood depended on how interpretations might affect self-evaluations. However, when the information was unambiguous, no differences in perceptions of sharing an esthetic preference were found. Whether the comparison target was superior or inferior, in both a positive and neutral mood, sharing a preference was regarded as highly reflective of similarity and participants assimilated to the targets.

## Experiment 4
Experiment 3 demonstrated that positive mood only leads to self-serving responding when the distinctive similarity information is ambiguous. Experiment 4 extends these finding by testing the hypothesis that asymmetric responding in a positive mood results from effortful reinterpretation of ambiguous information, after initial processing leads to detrimental results. To test this hypothesis, participants completed a mood induction exercise, were asked to complete a cognitively effortful task, and then viewed a comparison target with whom they shared a birthday.

As in Experiments 1 and 2, participants were provided with ambiguous similarity information. Reinterpretation of this information was only expected when such reinterpretation was necessary and when individuals had sufficient cognitive resources. Consequently, for participants not under cognitive load, replication of the positive mood conditions from Experiments 1 and 2 was expected. However, for participants under load, replication of the neutral mood conditions from Experiment 2 was expected; lack of cognitive resources was expected to disrupt reinterpretation of ambiguous similarity information, thus preventing participants from responding positively to the downward comparison condition.

## Method

## Participants and design
University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation. This experiment used a 2(mood: positive, neutral) × 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) × 2(load: load vs. no load) factorial design, with an additional no mood induction, no comparison, no load control condition.

## Procedure
The experimental procedures were the same as in Experiments 1 and 2. As in Experiment 1, participants completed either the happy or neutral mood exercise; there was no negative mood condition. Second, all participants viewed information about an attractive or unattractive comparison target which included information that they shared a birthday with the comparison target. Third, participants in the cognitive load conditions were asked to remember an 8-digit number and to be prepared to report the number when the experiment was finished (see Gilbert, Giesler, and Morris [1995]). Participants were not allowed to write down or otherwise record that number, but were asked to hold it in mind throughout the rest of the study. All participants were able to recall the number at the end of the session. Participants in the no load conditions were not given a number to rehearse.

After viewing the comparison targets, participants then completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2.

## Results and discussion
As in Experiment 2, a hanging control (no load, no mood, no comparison) condition was included in this study and the same analysis strategy was employed. First, a 2(load: load vs. no load) × 2(mood: positive, neutral) × 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) ANOVA was conducted, testing for main effects and interactions, followed by single degree of freedom contrasts to test specific hypotheses (Jaccard [1998]).

## Manipulation check
As expected, there was a main effect of mood induction on mood, F(1, 124) = 14.94, p < .001. Participants in the positive condition were more positive (M = 5.35, SD = .81) than participants in the neutral condition (M = 4.60, SD = .93). In addition, the attractive comparison target was rated more attractive than the (M = 5.58, SD = .78) than the unattractive target (M = 2.99, SD = .89), F(1,110) = 259.08, p < .001. No other effects on ratings of attractiveness or mood were significant, Fs < 1.

## Self-evaluations
Analysis revealed the expected three-way interaction effect of load, mood, and direction of comparison on attractiveness, F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001. The effects of load, F(1, 110) = 8.00, p = .006; mood F(1, 110) = 9.83, p = .002; direction, F(1, 110) = 135.31, p < .001; load and mood, F(1, 110) = 10.97, p = .001; load and direction, F(1, 110) = 10.44, p = .002 and mood and direction, F(1, 110) = 4.14, p = .04, were also significant.

For ease of interpreting the three-way interaction, the pattern of means is presented in Fig. 3, and the cognitive load and no load conditions are analyzed separately, with comparisons to the control condition.5

## No load conditions
All participants in the study believed they shared a birthday with the comparison targets; therefore, the positive mood conditions were expected to replicate the positive mood and shared-birthday conditions in Experiment 1.

The expected asymmetry among positive mood participants was found. Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found, regardless of whether participants upwardly compared (M = 5.64, SD = .78; F(1,124) = 17.39, p < .001) or downwardly compared (M = 5.15, SD = .81), F(1,124) = 11.90, p = .001.

The neutral mood conditions replicated previous findings of symmetric assimilation (Brown et al. [1992]). Upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.47, SD = .51) than the control condition, F(1,124) = 17.89, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings than the control condition (M = 3.24, SD = 1.09), F(1,124) = 10.37, p = .002.

Thus, positive mood led to asymmetric and self-serving responses, whereas neutral mood led to symmetric responses.

## Cognitive load conditions
Cognitive load was expected to disrupt the self-serving processing of participants in a positive mood, leading them to respond in the same manner as those in the neutral mood conditions.

As expected, cognitive load disrupted the self-serving responding associated with a positive mood. Instead, participants in a positive mood assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21), upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.71, SD = .83), F(1,124) = 23.14, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 3.09, SD = .94), t(124) = -3.30, p = .001. This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition.

Experiment 4 demonstrated that self-serving responding associated with positive mood is resource-dependent. When people in a positive mood were not under additional cognitive load, they adjusted their interpretations of the meaning of a shared birthday and responded to comparison targets in a self-serving ways, replicating Experiments 1 and 2. However, when cognitive resources were reduced, it was more difficult to adjust the interpretation of the meaning of a shared a birthday and, consequently, participants did not respond to comparisons in self-serving ways. Instead, their responses were like those of neutral mood participants: They assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Thus, when cognitive resources were lacking, the benefits of a positive mood were muted.

## General discussion
In four studies, positive mood led to self-serving interpretations of ambiguous similarity information. When participants were given ambiguous similarity information, they categorized targets in self-serving ways. If the comparison person was superior, they used the information to make the target distinctively similar, basked in that person’s glory, and boosted their self-evaluations. If the comparison person was inferior, they used the information to make the target either irrelevant or only generally similar, leading to no response to the comparison target or contrast of their self-evaluations with the inferior target. Overall, this pattern of self-serving responding was not found when the preference information was unambiguous or when participants were under cognitive loaded.

These studies establish that mood can determine how people interpret and respond to comparison information. These studies also revealed boundary conditions to self-serving responding that provide insight into the underlying processes. First, self-serving responses only occurred when individuals were given ambiguous or flexible information about the relation between themselves and a comparison target. In Experiment 1, when individuals were not told that they shared a birthday with the comparison targets, they were unable to respond in a self-serving manner. Likewise, in Experiment 3, when similarity information was unambiguous, they did not respond in a self-serving manner. Thus, while positive mood might provide cognitive flexibility, positive mood does not blind individuals from seeing negative information. In the absence of ambiguous information, self-serving responses did not arise.

Second, the effect only occurred when individuals had adequate cognitive resources. That cognitive load derailed the self-serving responses suggests that the flexible processing of comparison targets in positive moods is an effortful process and may be a correction process (e.g., Gilbert et al. [1995]; Stapel and Marx [2007]). In Experiment 4, in the absence of adequate cognitive resources, positive mood participants’ responses to the comparison targets were similar to the responses to neutral mood participants. That is, they were unable to make corrections or engage in reinterpretation of ambiguous information in order to avoid assimilation to the downward comparison target. This supports our suggestion of a two-step process in which individuals in a positive mood initially respond to social comparison information in a consistent manner, and only engage in effortful reanalysis of ambiguous information in order to correct for the negative influence of social comparison.

In addition, this finding contradicts an alternative explanation that our effects are the result of positive moods inducing heuristic processing and negative moods inducing systematic processing. If heuristic processing were responsible for how participants responded to the comparisons, we would expect the same level of processing of both upward and downward comparisons, with symmetric contrast (or assimilation) to both types of targets. However, positive moods led to the use of a trivial similarity cue to indicate similarity in the upward comparison condition but not in the downward comparison conditions. In addition, if heuristic processing were responsible for the effects in the positive mood conditions, then inducing cognitive load should not have eliminated the self-serving pattern.

Third, we found asymmetry only under positive mood, not under negative mood. If self-serving responses were only defensive, we might have found that negative mood, an aversive state, would have led to an interpretation of information that allowed for recovery. Alternatively, if responses resulted from mood-congruent information search and processing, we would expect that negative mood should lead to asymmetrically negative responses. Instead, negative mood was associated with processing of information with greater neutrality, objectivity, and focus on the data at hand, regardless of the consequence for self-evaluations (for reviews see Bless [2001]; Martin and Clore [2001]).

Finally, the results of the present studies suggest that asymmetric responses are not a result of using mood as a resource (Trope et al. [2001]). According to this model, a positive mood can be a treated as resource to be expended in the pursuit of accurate information. If this were true, in this case, we would have expected that positive mood would have been associated with contrastive responses to comparison targets, a response that is associated with information-seeking motives (Stapel and Koomen [2001a]). Indeed, in other research, the experience of self-affirmation is related to just such symmetric responses to comparisons (Johnson and Stapel, in press).

In sum, these findings support the growing body of literature showing that positive moods can create an upward spiral (Fredrickson and Joiner [2002]). Numerous cognitive processes are associated with positive mood and in responding to social comparison information; among these the ability to make fine distinctions between distinctive similarity and general similarity may be particularly helpful. Individuals in a positive mood were able to convert what could be considered negative feedback (one is less attractive than another person) into positive self-evaluations. Positive mood granted individuals the ability to see a shared-birthday or a shared-artistic preference as meaningful indicators of shared distinctiveness and similarity, allowing them to assimilate to upward comparison targets. Positive mood also granted individuals the ability to recognize a shared-birthday a meaningless indicator of similarity, and allowed them to contrast with downward comparison targets.

Future research might investigate how dispositional happiness might be related to the self-serving bias presented here. If positive emotions do create an upward spiral, consistently interpreting ambiguity in self-serving ways might one way in which dispostionally happy people are able to reap self-evaluative boosts from downward comparisons and are buffered from the self-depreciating effects of upward comparisons (Lyubomirsky and Ross [1997]).

## Conclusions
It has become increasingly clear that while social comparisons may be ubiquitous, the impact of social comparison information is highly dependent upon the contexts within which comparisons arise and the motivations of the individuals involved. The present studies add to the existing literature by highlighting how mood can influence how individuals treat similarity cues in their environment, such as social comparison information. In the presence of a positive mood, ambiguous social comparison information is interpreted in a self-serving manner, such that positive self-evaluations result. Thus, a good mood can beget not only a good mood, but also beget a more positive self-image.

headline.statement: Experiment 4's control condition is reported as mean 4.20 with a standard deviation of 0.21 on a seven-point single-item rating, a pair no sample of whole-number ratings can produce at any group size tested, and every one of that experiment's eight comparisons is measured against it.
headline.evidence: "Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found, regardless of whether participants upwardly compared (M = 5.64, SD = .78; F(1,124) = 17.39, p < .001) or downwardly compared (M = 5.15, SD = .81), F(1,124) = 11.90, p = .001." The same pair is repeated in the load section: "Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21)". The measure is stated: participants "completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2", and Experiment 1 prints "a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)". GRIMMER returns impossible at n = 10, 15, 20, 25 and 75, under both the sample (n-1) and population (n) SD conventions, and with the scale bounds removed entirely (feasible_ignoring_bounds: false). SPRITE returns no_solution_proven. R's rsprite2 independently refuses the parameters with "fails GRIMMER test".
headline.plain: In the fourth experiment, the comparison group everything else is measured against is reported with an average of 4.20 and a spread of 0.21. Because each person gave a single whole-number rating from 1 to 7, only certain combinations of average and spread are arithmetically possible, and this one is not -- at any group size we tried, and under either of the two standard ways of calculating spread. Two separate pieces of software agree. All eight of that experiment's reported comparisons are measured against this pair of numbers.

findings.title: Experiment 4's control mean and SD (4.20, 0.21) cannot arise from whole-number ratings at any group size tested
findings.location: Experiment 4, No load conditions and Cognitive load conditions
findings.reported: "Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found"; repeated verbatim in the load section as "Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21)". Experiment 4's Procedure states participants "completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2"; Experiment 1's Dependent measures prints "a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)".
findings.computed: GRIMMER returns `impossible` at n = 10, 15, 20, 25 and 75. At n = 15 the only mean-consistent integer total is 63, and no integer sum-of-squares of the required parity falls in the window [265.19, 265.25] that SD = 0.21 implies. Every run reports feasible_ignoring_bounds: false, population_feasible_ignoring_bounds: false -- so the verdict does not depend on the 1-7 range at all, nor on which SD convention is used. sprite_reconstruct returns outcome `no_solution_proven`: "No integer sample can produce this mean/SD pair." R's rsprite2 independently refuses the same parameters with "The standard deviation is not consistent with this mean and number of observations (fails GRIMMER test)". Two engines, agreeing.
findings.assumptions: That each participant contributed one whole-number rating, which the paper establishes by stating Experiment 4 used the same single-item attractiveness measure as Experiments 1 and 2, whose numerals are printed. The control group's size is NOT printed and the experiment's own degrees of freedom disagree about it (see the sample-size finding), which is why five candidate values spanning 10 to 75 were tested; all five fail. Scale bounds are not load-bearing. The two commonest innocent explanations are closed by the sweep's own tallies: across the paper's 13 granularity checks, none is rescued by truncation rather than round-half rounding, and none by the population rather than the sample SD.

consequence.explanation: This control condition is the baseline for all eight of Experiment 4's reported contrasts, including the four that carry its central claim that cognitive load abolishes self-serving responding.

findings.plain: The fourth experiment compares eight groups against one no-treatment comparison group, reported as averaging 4.20 with a spread of 0.21. Each participant gave a single whole-number score from 1 to 7, and that restricts which average-and-spread combinations can exist. This one cannot exist -- we tested group sizes from 10 to 75, both standard formulas for spread, and with the 1-to-7 limits removed; it failed every time, and a second, independent piece of statistical software reached the same conclusion. The paper does not say how many people were in this group, so we could not test the one true size, but no size we tried works. Every conclusion the fourth experiment draws is measured against these two numbers.

findings.title: Two Table 2 cells report a standard deviation of .52 that no set of twelve whole-number ratings can produce
findings.location: Table 2, Self-evaluation row, Positive/Unambiguous Upward and Positive/Unambiguous Downward
findings.reported: Table 2 prints "6.58 (.52)" and "4.08 (.52)" for the two Positive/Unambiguous self-evaluation cells. Experiment 3's Procedure states participants "rated their own attractiveness (on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2)"; both of those experiments print a single seven-point item.
findings.computed: GRIMMER returns `impossible` for both cells at n = 12. For 6.58 the only mean-consistent total is 79 and no integer sum-of-squares of matching parity falls in the implied window; for 4.08 the only total is 49, same result. Both runs report feasible_ignoring_bounds: false, and re-running both cells with the range set to 1-9 instead of 1-7 returns `impossible` unchanged -- the scale is not load-bearing. R's rsprite2 refuses both cells with "fails GRIMMER test". Both are near misses: the sweep records .51 as the only attainable SD where .52 is printed, in both cells.
findings.assumptions: The cell size of 12 is DERIVED, not printed: Experiment 3 states "University students (N = 96)" in a fully crossed 2 x 2 x 2 design, and its ANOVA error df of 88 plus 8 cells returns 96. The derivation is corroborated -- all eight Table 2 self-evaluation means pass GRIM at n = 12, which a wrong denominator would not generally produce, and the planned comparisons carry df of 94. If the cells were in fact unequal this finding does not stand, and that is the single assumption a reader must accept. That both cells miss by one hundredth invites a rounding convention we have not reproduced, but the sweep's tally records no cell in this paper rescued by truncation, and it would have to be the same unreproduced convention twice.

consequence.explanation: These are the two cells of the Positive/Unambiguous contrast reported as F(1, 94) = 92.47, p < .001, the result establishing that unambiguous similarity information produces symmetric assimilation.

findings.plain: Two cells of the third experiment's results table report a spread of .52 among twelve people's whole-number ratings. No set of twelve whole numbers gives that spread alongside the averages printed beside it -- the closest achievable value is .51, in both cells. A second, independent piece of software agrees. This holds whether the rating scale ran 1 to 7 or 1 to 9. The one thing we had to work out for ourselves is that each cell held twelve people, which follows from the stated total of 96 split across eight groups and is supported by all eight averages in that row being achievable at twelve. These two cells are the ones behind one of the experiment's headline comparisons.

findings.title: Experiment 3 reports a mean rating of 7.33 on an instrument it states was the seven-point scale of Experiments 1 and 2
findings.reported: Procedure: "Participants reported their major, gender, age, and then rated their own attractiveness (on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2). Then, participants rated the target on her attractiveness." Manipulation check: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001." Experiment 1 prints "a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)" and "the same 7-point scale"; Experiment 2 prints "seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)".
findings.computed: grim_check returns `impossible` with failure_mode `out_of_range`: at n = 48 the mean implies a total of 352 against a maximum attainable total of 336 on a 1-7 scale. The mean is above the ceiling irrespective of n. R's scrutiny returns `consistent`, and the two engines do not conflict -- scrutiny tests granularity only, which our own run also passes; the impossibility is the range violation, which scrutiny does not test. recalc_anova separately confirms the printed F is exactly what these two means and SDs imply (calculated F = 169.24, achievable interval [166.76, 171.75] against a reported 170.34), so the arithmetic is internally coherent and the conflict is with the instrument.
findings.assumptions: The seven-point range is imported into Experiment 3 by the paper's own cross-reference rather than printed in Experiment 3 itself, and the sentence carrying that cross-reference contains a typo ("seam" for "same"). The innocent explanation is live and the paper does not close it: Experiment 3 may have run on nine-point instruments -- its own similarity items are printed as nine-point, as are the pilot's -- in which case the value is fine and the Procedure misdescribes the measure. Experiment 3's mood mean in the same paragraph is also 7.33, on a mood measure whose range the paper never states at all. Severity is set below `impossible` for exactly this reason: the contradiction between the two passages is certain, but which of them is wrong is not.

consequence.explanation: Experiment 3's direction-of-comparison manipulation check rests on a mean that the instrument the paper names cannot produce; either that check is wrong or the Methods misdescribe the measure.

findings.plain: The third experiment says it measured attractiveness using the same seven-point scale as the earlier experiments, then reports an average rating of 7.33 -- higher than the scale's maximum. One of those two statements must be wrong. It may simply be that this experiment actually used a nine-point scale and the methods section describes it incorrectly, which is plausible because the same experiment's other questions are on nine-point scales and the sentence in question contains a spelling error. We cannot tell which, so we report the contradiction rather than calling the number impossible.

findings.title: Experiment 4 states 193 participants but its degrees of freedom account for roughly 133, with no exclusions reported
findings.location: Experiment 4, Participants and design vs Results and discussion
findings.reported: "University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation." The contrasts throughout are reported on F(1, 124) over nine groups; the factorial is reported on F(1, 110) over eight cells.
findings.computed: check_summation_batch, applying the paper's own reconciliation rule (error df plus number of groups equals analysed N) to all five studies: the pilot (42 + 3 = 45), Experiment 1 (43 + 4 = 47), Experiment 2 (132 + 9 = 141) and Experiment 3 (88 + 8 = 96) all land exactly on their stated totals. Experiment 4 gives 124 + 9 = 133 against a stated 193, a shortfall of 60. Its internal figures are mutually coherent -- 110 + 8 = 118 in the factorial, plus a control of 15, is 133 -- so the stated N is the sole outlier.
findings.assumptions: That the error df of a single-degree-of-freedom contrast over nine groups is N minus 9. This is not an assumption imposed from outside: it is validated on four other studies in the same paper, where it reproduces each stated total exactly. A typo in the printed N (193 for 133) would account for the whole gap and is the least dramatic reading.

consequence.explanation: Every test reported in Experiment 4 runs on degrees of freedom implying about 133 analysed participants, so on the stated recruitment roughly 60 people are silently absent from every analysis.

findings.plain: The fourth experiment says 193 people took part, but the statistics reported for it are calculated as though about 133 people were analysed -- roughly 60 short. No exclusions are described anywhere, and the one obvious reason for excluding people is explicitly ruled out: the paper says every participant successfully recalled the memory-load number. The same arithmetic, applied to the paper's other four studies, matches their stated totals exactly, so this is not a quirk of how we counted. A typing error in the printed total would explain it entirely.

findings.title: The two means in Experiment 4's central conclusion run opposite to the labels attached to them
findings.location: Experiment 4, Cognitive load conditions, final sentence
findings.reported: "This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition." The control mean given two sentences earlier is 4.20.
findings.computed: Ordering each printed mean against the control mean printed in the same passage: the mean labelled "more positive" (3.33) is below the control (4.20) and the mean labelled "less positive" (5.53) is above it. The other three pairs in the same two paragraphs run the correct way -- positive mood under load gives 5.71 above and 3.09 below; no-load neutral gives 5.47 above and 3.24 below. Verified verbatim in the XML full text.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed values. The F statistics do not disambiguate which mean belongs to which condition. Figure 3 plots these means and would settle whether this is a writing error or a data error; the figure was not read.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a reading of the paper's prose against its own printed means, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: The sentence asserts that positive mood under load becomes indistinguishable from neutral mood, which is Experiment 4's central claim, but as printed the neutral-mood means it cites run the opposite way to the description.

findings.plain: The sentence carrying the fourth experiment's main conclusion describes one group as having rated themselves more positively than the comparison group and another as less positively -- but the numbers printed alongside those words say the reverse. The most likely explanation is that the two figures were swapped when the sentence was written, which is a proofreading failure rather than a data problem. As printed, though, the sentence does not support the claim it makes.

findings.title: Experiment 3's headline contrasts imply standardised effects near five standard deviations on single-item rating scales
findings.location: Table 2, Self-evaluation and Similarity rows, positive mood columns
findings.reported: Table 2 gives Positive/Unambiguous self-evaluations of 6.58 (.52) upward versus 4.08 (.52) downward, and Positive/Ambiguous similarity of 7.06 (.53) upward versus 4.14 (.59) downward, at twelve per cell. The paper prints no effect size of its own.
findings.computed: check_effect_plausibility gives Hedges' g = 4.64, 95% CI [3.23, 6.39] for the self-evaluation contrast and g = 5.03, 95% CI [3.53, 6.88] for the similarity contrast. The tool reports the magnitude and declines to judge it: "|d| = 4.64 is remarkable in any field." Separately, required_n shows a two-group comparison would need 26 per group to detect d = 0.8 at 80% power, against the 12 per group available here.
findings.assumptions: This escalation above the tool's own `consistent` verdict is a reviewer-supplied judgement under rulebook rule 6, not a determination by the tool; the comparison class -- that standardised effects near g = 5 are far outside what social-psychological rating measures ordinarily yield -- is mine, and the paper never accepted it. Of the three ordinary causes, a units mismatch is ruled out (both rows are the paper's own rating scales) and a waitlist comparator does not apply (these are randomised between-subjects cells), but dispersion reported as standard error rather than standard deviation cannot be fully ruled out: neither table carries a footnote defining the parenthetical value, and the reading as SD comes from the prose, which writes "M = x, SD = y" for the same quantities. If those parentheses were standard errors, these effect sizes are inflated.

consequence.explanation: The two contrasts the paper leans on in Experiment 3 imply differences of roughly five standard deviations, which is the combination -- very large observed effects from twelve people per cell -- in which estimates are most inflated.

findings.plain: The differences between groups in the third experiment are enormous by the standards of this kind of research: the two groups barely overlap at all. Effects that large from twelve people per group are the pattern you see when results have been selected or when something has gone wrong upstream, though they are not impossible on their own. One caveat cuts the other way: neither table explains what the numbers in brackets are, and if they are a different measure of variability than we assumed, these effects would be considerably smaller. This is a judgement we are supplying, not a standard the paper set for itself.

findings.title: Malformed test statistics in results-carrying sentences: two p-values printed with no decimal point and a degrees-of-freedom value matching no group structure
findings.location: Experiment 1, Self-evaluations; Experiment 4, Self-evaluations and Manipulation check
findings.reported: Experiment 1: "Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011." Experiment 4: "Analysis revealed the expected three-way interaction effect of load, mood, and direction of comparison on attractiveness, F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001." Experiment 4 manipulation check: "the attractive comparison target was rated more attractive than the (M = 5.58, SD = .78) than the unattractive target (M = 2.99, SD = .89)".
findings.computed: As printed, "p = 011" and "p = 001" are not p-values; no recomputation against them is possible, so both statistics are unverifiable as published. The error df of 46 in Experiment 1 corresponds to no group structure the experiment describes: the 2 x 2 ANOVA reported two sentences earlier uses F(1, 43), where 43 is 47 minus 4 cells, and a two-group comparison of 47 participants would give 45. All three passages are present identically in the XML full text.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed text. "p = 011" is almost certainly ".011", which is what F(1, 43) = 6.95 would give, and "p = 001" almost certainly ".001"; on those readings only the notation is wrong. Grouped as one finding because all three sit in results-carrying sentences and evidence the same thing -- that the Results were not closely proofread.

consequence.explanation: Two of the paper's reported effects -- Experiment 1's symmetric-contrast simple effect and Experiment 4's three-way interaction, which is that experiment's primary result -- are reported with p-values that are not p-values as printed.

findings.plain: Two of the paper's significance values are printed without their decimal points, so as they stand they are not percentages or probabilities at all; one of them belongs to the fourth experiment's main result. In the first experiment, a comparison is also reported using a sample-size figure that does not match any grouping the experiment describes. These are almost certainly typesetting or typing errors rather than data problems, but they mean the reader cannot check those two results as published.

findings.title: A reported p of .83 where the printed F statistic implies .22
findings.location: Experiment 3, Perceptions of similarity, final sentence
findings.reported: "Identical effects emerged when the information was unambiguous, F(1, 94) = 1.50, p = .83."
findings.computed: recalc_f_to_p gives p = 0.2237 for F(1, 94) = 1.50, with an achievable interval of [0.2230, 0.2245] given the printed precision -- far outside any rounding window around .83. statcheck flags the same pair as an inconsistency. The two tools formally disagree: recalc_f_to_p returns `consistent` because it is deliberately directional and flags only p-values SMALLER than the statistic supports, treating a larger one as conservative reporting. The severity here rests on statcheck's flag together with the size of the gap, not on overriding the directional tool.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's printed values. An adjustment for multiple comparisons would raise a p-value, but the paper reports no correction for Experiment 3; a typo in the printed .83 is the likelier explanation. The sentence describes this effect as "identical" to the F(1, 94) = .31, p = .58 result immediately preceding it, which recomputes exactly.

consequence.explanation: Both the reported and the recomputed value are far above the .05 threshold, so the 'no difference' conclusion the sentence draws is unaffected and only the printed number is wrong.

findings.plain: One reported result gives a significance value of .83 where the test statistic printed beside it implies about .22. The conclusion drawn from it -- that there was no difference -- is the same either way, so nothing in the paper's argument turns on it, but one of the two numbers is wrong.

findings.title: The pilot's self-evaluation ANOVA is reported with one numerator degree of freedom for a three-group comparison
findings.reported: "Those in the negative mood (M = 6.98, SD = .53), positive mood (M = 6.98, SD = .80), and the control condition (M = 6.82, SD = .67), did not differ F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76."
findings.computed: The same paragraph reports the mood ANOVA over the same three groups as F(2, 42), so the numerator degrees of freedom for a three-group one-way comparison is 2 and the printed 1 is a misprint. recalc_f_to_p run at both readings settles which number is wrong: the printed p of .76 falls inside the achievable interval [0.761, 0.768] at df1 = 2, and does not reconcile at df1 = 1, which implies p = .606.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed text. The finding rests on the contradiction between two sentences in the same paragraph, with the two recomputations as supporting evidence; recalc_f_to_p itself returns `consistent` on the printed pairing because it is directional and treats an over-large p as conservative reporting.

consequence.explanation: The claim is a null one -- that mood alone did not move self-evaluations -- and it holds under either reading, so the error is in the notation rather than the conclusion.

findings.plain: In the pilot study, a comparison across three groups is reported using a figure that only fits a two-group comparison, while the sentence just above it reports the correct figure for three groups. The conclusion is unaffected -- the groups did not differ either way -- but the notation is wrong.

findings.title: The pilot's mood ANOVA reports F = 18.44 where its own printed means and SDs imply about 26.5
findings.reported: "A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) revealed that the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001," alongside group means of 7.20 (SD .93), 6.15 (SD .52) and 4.98 (SD .98).
findings.computed: rivets_anova, run at three equal groups of 15, gives an achievable F interval of [26.01, 27.04] across the rounding box of the printed inputs, with a point value of 26.48. The reported 18.44 lies outside that interval. The tool returned `highly_suspicious`; it is recorded a rung lower here.
findings.assumptions: The group sizes are OUR inference, not the paper's. The pilot states only "N = 45" across three conditions and never prints cell sizes; the equal split of 15/15/15 follows from 45 dividing by three and from the error df of 42 confirming three groups totalling 45, but unequal cells would change the achievable interval and could reconcile the reported value. Rulebook rule 4 caps an assumption-dependent finding at `suspicious`, which is why the tool's own verdict is not carried through, and why this cannot be the paper's headline problem.

consequence.explanation: The reported statistic is smaller than the printed means and SDs support, so the mood manipulation check is if anything understated and the manipulation is significant on either value.

findings.plain: In the pilot study, the test statistic reported for the mood manipulation is smaller than the group averages printed beside it can produce -- about 18 where roughly 26 is implied. This works against the authors rather than for them, since the larger value would be a stronger result. The comparison depends on our assuming the 45 participants split evenly into three groups of 15, which the paper does not state, so it is a question rather than a determination.

findings.title: Table 1's caption names three dependent measures; the table reports one and Experiment 2 analyses only that one
findings.location: Table 1 caption vs Table 1 body and Experiment 2, Dependent measures
findings.reported: Caption: "Effects of upward (more attractive) versus downward (less attractive) comparisons on self-evaluations, ratings of target similarity, and use of information to benefit the self as a function of mood and shared birthday information." The table body carries a single row, labelled Self-evaluation.
findings.computed: Both the XML grid and the PDF grid return exactly one body row for Table 1, so this is not an extraction failure. Experiment 2's Dependent measures section describes only attractiveness ratings of self and target plus a single mood item -- no similarity index and no 'use of information' measure -- and the Results section analyses neither of the two additional measures the caption names.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own text. The likeliest explanation is that the caption was copied from Table 2, which does carry a Similarity row, or from a template. The alternative and more consequential reading is that measures were collected and not reported.

consequence.explanation: Two dependent measures the caption says the table reports appear nowhere in it, and Experiment 2's Results analyse neither, so two measures named as reported are absent.

findings.plain: The heading above the second experiment's results table promises three sets of measurements; the table contains one, and the experiment's text never analyses the other two. The methods section for that experiment also never describes collecting them. Most likely the heading was copied from the other table in the paper, which does contain one of the missing measures. The less comfortable possibility is that measurements were taken and not reported.

findings.title: The paper's only route to its underlying data is a footnote directing readers to one author
findings.reported: "Complete data and results available from the first author."
findings.computed: The paper deposits nothing: no repository, no accession number, no supplementary file, and none accompanies the article. This is the paper's sole data provision.
findings.assumptions: A 'data available on request' footnote was entirely conventional for a 2011 psychology article and is not, in that era, a departure from any standard the paper or its field then imposed; it is graded `indeterminate` for that reason and should not be read as a criticism of the authors' practice at the time. It is recorded because it is the only route by which the arithmetic anomalies above could be settled, and because the article has since been retracted, which makes that route uncertain.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a reading of the paper's reporting practice, not a calculation.

consequence.explanation: None of the granularity anomalies in this report can be resolved without the underlying data, and the paper provides no route to it independent of an author's cooperation.

findings.plain: The paper says its data can be obtained by writing to the first author. That was normal practice for a psychology paper in 2011 and is not a criticism. It matters only because the arithmetic problems described above could be settled immediately by the raw ratings, and no copy of those ratings was deposited anywhere.

not_checked.reason: No cell size is printed and none can be derived: the factorial holds 126 participants (error df 118 plus 8 cells) across 8 cells, and 126 does not divide by 8, so the cells are provably unequal. check_table refused all 24 candidate checks for want of a denominator. Guessing one here is the standard route to a false accusation, so Experiment 2's entire results table is outside the reach of this analysis and nothing in this report clears it.

The similarity index is the mean of three nine-point items, so its granularity is one thirty-sixth rather than one twelfth. Our GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE implementations take no items parameter, so checking these at the wrong step size would manufacture impossibilities; the dispatcher correctly refused all 8. An implementation taking an items argument, such as R's scrutiny, could check them.

not_checked.location: Pilot study, mood index and self-evaluation index means

This article reports a pilot study and four between-subjects experiments arguing that positive mood lets people reinterpret ambiguous similarity information in self-serving ways: assimilating to superior comparison targets, contrasting away from inferior ones, and losing the ability to do either under cognitive load. It is marked RETRACTED on every page of the record. This analysis is an arithmetic check of the document as published and takes no position on the retraction or on the responsibility of either author.

Forty-two checks ran. Twenty-four passed, twenty of those collapsed inside a single table dispatch and therefore invisible in the findings list: all eight of Table 2's self-evaluation means are attainable at twelve per cell, six of those eight also survive both dispersion checks, Experiment 3's manipulation-check F recomputes almost exactly from its own printed means, and statcheck's own count of decision errors -- results whose significance verdict changes on recomputation -- is zero across the twenty-two statistics it could parse. That last number deserves saying plainly, because the raw statcheck count of twenty flagged rows badly overstates the problem: eighteen of them are rounding, .008 against a computed .007877 and the like. Multiplicity is also not a problem here. Experiment 3's planned comparisons lose nothing to any of the four standard corrections, and footnotes 2 and 5 record that Experiments 2 and 4 were re-run with Tukey's HSD with the changed contrast named -- more discipline than most papers of this vintage show.

What does not hold together is concentrated, and it is concentrated in Experiment 4. Its control condition is reported twice as 4.20 with a spread of 0.21, and no sample of whole-number ratings produces that pair -- not at any of the five group sizes tested, not under either formula for the standard deviation, and not with the scale limits removed, which is the strongest form this check takes because it means the verdict does not rest on any range at all. Its stated recruitment of 193 exceeds what its own degrees of freedom account for by about sixty people, with no exclusion reported and the obvious exclusion route explicitly closed by the paper's statement that every participant recalled the load number. Its primary three-way interaction is printed "p = 001". And the sentence carrying its central conclusion -- that positive mood under load becomes indistinguishable from neutral mood -- attaches "more positive" to a mean below the control and "less positive" to one above it. Any one of those is an ordinary publishing accident. Together, in one experiment, they mean nothing that experiment reports can be verified as printed.

The Table 2 anomaly is narrower and cleaner. Two cells share the printed dispersion .52 where the only value twelve whole-number ratings can produce is .51, and they are the two cells behind the contrast the paper reports as F(1, 94) = 92.47. Both engines agree, and the result is unchanged whether the scale ran to 7 or to 9. The single thing a reader must accept is that the cells held twelve people each, which we derived rather than read; the corroboration is that all eight means in that row are attainable at twelve, which a wrong denominator does not generally deliver.

Three things cut the other way and belong in the same breath. First, the Experiment 3 off-scale mean of 7.33 is a contradiction between two passages, not a demonstrated impossibility: the paper never prints Experiment 3's own scale, importing it by a cross-reference in a sentence that contains a typo, and the alternative -- that the experiment ran on nine-point instruments throughout, as its similarity items demonstrably do -- would leave the number fine and the Methods wrong. Second, the pilot's out-of-range F rests on our assuming its 45 participants split evenly in three, which the paper does not state. Third, the very large effect sizes in Experiment 3, near five standard deviations, are a comparison we are supplying and would shrink substantially if the values in parentheses turned out to be standard errors -- neither table says which they are.

The coverage limits matter as much as the findings. Experiment 2's entire results table could not be checked at all: 126 participants do not divide into eight cells, no cell sizes are printed, and guessing a denominator is the standard route to a false accusation. Table 2's eight similarity cells are three-item composites our implementations cannot check at the right step size. Every cell mean in Experiments 2 and 4 reported in prose is likewise beyond reach. None of that clears those numbers; it means they were not examined.

Two independently impossible mean-and-standard-deviation pairs, each sitting under a result the paper depends on, are not reconcilable with the rest of what the paper reports. I have no confidence in the accuracy of Experiment 4 as published, and the Table 2 cells warrant the same reservation; the paper's own numbers do not reconcile.
